turn_text: This is Capitol Cast from Capitol News, Illinois. I'm Jennifer Fuller. We're continuing our influential Illinoisan series this week with a conversation with former U.S. Representative Sherry Bustos. The Quad Cities Democrat has a long pedigree in Illinois politics and put that to use in Washington.

You know, I was really so lucky to have a great mom and dad. And the way my dad, who was particularly influential in my life, he always said to my sister and to me, and we had a brother and my sister and me, was that we could do whatever the heck we wanted to do. And he also taught us that we are no better than anybody, but nor are we any worse than anybody. So it's like I just always had that in my mind and I cannot think of a time with one exception that I felt intimidated or shy around any man or felt less than any man. I just like, and again, I feel so lucky and I would say if there's something I could bestow and wish upon any younger person, it would be self-confidence. But other than that, I just, I feel like I've got a healthy level of self-confidence. And I've also got, to your earlier point, I have a healthy level of ambition. turn_text: You mentioned your dad, who was one of the more influential political voices in the room. You have a political pedigree. When did you know you wanted to go into political life?

Well, I actually did not plan to run for office. I've been around politics my whole life. So my dad, his name was Gene Callahan. He passed away in 2014. But his political background was he was a journalist, wrote a five day a week political column out of Springfield, Illinois for the newspaper. At the time it was the register. Now it's the journal register. At one point went to his boss and said he needed a raise because there were he had three kids and he couldn't afford Having three kids and the editor said, well, Jane, you're already the best paid reporter in the news or I can't pay you anymore. And so he had to leave because he just like literally he and my mom couldn't afford us. And so he works for Governor Kerner back in the, so this goes way back. So the listeners will have to go the way back in their memory or they probably don't might not even have a memory, but he was a deputy press secretary. And then a guy named Sam Shapiro was the governor and he was his deputy press secretary. And then there was a guy named Paul Simon. who was running for a lieutenant governor. My dad became his chief of staff. And so, and Paul Simon hired a guy named Dick Durban, who was fresh out of law school. And so, my dad was Dick Durban's boss. And at one point, Paul Simon lived with our family. Then my dad would go on to work for a guy named Alan Dixon, who was the state treasurer, then Secretary of State and then U.S. Senator. So we have been around Democratic politicians since I was a little girl. And my grandpa was a state legislator. He was a hog farmer out of Iroquois County, which is a very Republican county, but he was a Democrat. So he was a state legislator and because we grew up in Springfield, my grandma and grandpa would stay with us when the legislature was in session. So, you know, all of this, I share all of this because these are the best, just great memories. My dad was the kind of guy who never shoot us away and would say, this is an adult conversation. You can't be here. Never did he do that. And my price of admission to sitting at the table alongside some of these legends was I would have to go to the refrigerator and pop a Budweiser forum. And I just don't remember, I'd go behind, this is probably my love of a beer to this day, but I'd duck my head down and take a quick swig and then go deliver the can of Bud to him. So I just would sit there and listen and just was fascinated by all these stories. That said, I was a political science major. but never thought I would run for office. I just, I wanted to be around people who I loved. And like these are people I loved. I just, I was fascinated by them and always, you know, we talked about being an elected official in the highest of terms. Like this was a calling, this was, these are good, honorable people. And they were always, my dad always talked about helping people. It was always through that lens. So I thought I just want to work for, for good people. So major in political science, I went to University of Maryland and got out and I interned with the Illinois State Senate. And I hated it. I mean, like I hated, I sat in a room with three other interns, two of whom I keep in touch with to this day and my friends. But we sat in this room, little bitty room, no windows and analyzed bills. all day. So we'd get these 20, 30, 40, 50 page bills and we'd have to write a one page synopsis. And I literally like, this is politics. This isn't, you know, I like to go to the events and I like to talk to people and I like to be around people and I want to help people. And so I finished that internship and it's like, I'm kind of heartbroken because I majored in this. I think this is what I want to do and I hate it. So I go back to school to the program, actually that Paul Simon founded, and you're aware of it because you went through the Public Affairs Reporting Program. But it's called Public Affairs Reporting. And now it's called University of Illinois at Springfield. And it's a journalism program. It's covering the kind of people that I knew growing up. And so I became a journalist. And by the way, a side note, I had two job offers at the end of my internship. One was at the Southern Illinois Inn here in Carbondale. And the other one was at the Quad City Times in Davenport, Iowa. So I ended up taking the Quad City Times. I always lived in the Illinois Quad Cities, though, because it's like Illinois is my home. I plan to live in Illinois the rest of my life. So I lived in Moline, Illinois, would cross the Mississippi River every day to go into work. and became a journalist. And as you know, when you're a journalist, you can't do anything politically. You cover everybody. You cover, you know, whether it's the state legislature, which I started out doing in the internship, and then covered the police beat and then City Hall, and but covered people who were running for office. So for 17 years, I was a journalist for 17 years, did not pound a yard sign. did not go to a political fundraiser, did not make a political contribution, did not knock any doors, did not do anything politically, except for a vote. And so to your question, I did not plan to run for office, and certainly I thought I'd be a journalist the rest of my life, just zero plans to ever run for office.

turn_text: You touched on this a little bit. You navigated a time as you were in Congress where there were a lot of people saying, I'm not going to do this anymore. Well, I think you always have to have hope. I still have hope today, even though politics, even in my 10 years in the U.S. House of Representatives, it changed a lot. Think about, I was in from 2013, January of 2013 to January of 2023. think about in that time. You had Barack Obama just elected to a second term. Four years later, again, the 17-point swing in the congressional district I represented, then the public elects Donald Trump. And then four years after that, the public elects Joe Biden. And right before swearing in, or before the inauguration, right after two days after that term, the members who were elected to the House and the Senate were sworn in. You have, January 6th happened, three days after. And so that is a, you can, I certainly understand why someone like Jerry Costello said it was time to move on. Jerry's a dear friend of our families. I have great respect for him. I was just with John Shim because a couple weeks ago at the, right outside the Farm Progress Show up in Decatur. They're both good men, different politics, very different politics between the two of them. But for me, you know, it took 10 years and actually January 6 was the last straw for my family. They were at home and watching, I actually sent them a text. We were on a, you know, we have a family text and I said, just want to let you know I'm okay. I mean, it is life-changing when you've got an angry group of people who want to come in and disrupt Democracy, I guess, if you want to look at that in the most simplest of terms. But where you've got the police officer telling you to get ready to get on the floor, get ready to put on your gas masks, getting evacuated from the house or the floor of the US House of Representatives. You know, so it just changes your life and really your outlook. But again, I can't say that that was my last straw. But for my family, it was. We had a family meeting on Easter after that happened. And but the consensus was, Hey, you're, you know, by Washington standard, you're a baby, you know, I saw plenty of life and energy and all of that. And they just said, there's other things you can do with your with your abilities. So I made the decision. It was, gosh, probably just a within a few weeks, I made the announcement that it wasn't running for reelection.
